We estimate the parameters in equation (7) using a Bayesian logistic regression that
pools participants’ choices from the signals and all treatments.
Figure K.3 summarizes the main results from the estimation of equation (7). The left
panel reports the posterior distribution of the probability of a correct action under the
signals and all treatments, averaging across participants, games, and rounds, while holding
fixed the information from signals (log-oddsit) and others’ actions (sharev−i,t−1) at their
median values in the data. We find a significant increase in performance of 6 percentage
points when participants are assigned to the all treatment relative to the signals treatment,
that cannot be directly attributed to the informational value of signals or others’ actions.
67


## Page 68


The middle panel reports the effect of signals on performance by treatment. We show
the probability of a correct action as log-oddscorrect
it
varies from its minimum to its maximum
in the data, while holding others’ actions (sharev−i,t−1) fixed at their median values. For
participants in both the signals and all treatments, performance improves substantially as
signals become more informative about the true state. This effect is stronger for participants
in the all treatment, particularly when signals are less informative.
The right panel isolates the effect of others’ actions on performance by reporting the
probability of a correct action as sharev−i,t−1 varies from zero to one, while holding the
informativeness of signals (log-oddscorrect
it
) fixed at its median value. Consistent with the
results in the main text (Observation 2), participants in the all treatment improve their
performance by relying on the redundant information conveyed by others’ actions. This
improvement remains substantial even after accounting for the informativeness of observed
signals, increasing the probability of a correct action by more than 10 percentage points as
the share of others’ correct actions in the previous round rises from zero to one.
Using the estimated parameters, we construct a baseline predicted probability of a
correct action driven only by variation across participants and games (αig), rounds (λt),
and treatments (δtreat[i]), setting β1 = β2 = 0 and thereby shutting down the contribution of
both signals and others’ actions.
We then construct predicted probabilities driven by signals by adding to the baseline
specification the information provided by signals, β1 log-oddscorrect
it
, while keeping β2 = 0.
Finally, we construct predicted probabilities driven by signals + actions by augmenting
the signals specification with the effect of others’ actions, β2 sharev−i,t−1.
Figure K.4 reports, for each game round, the additional informational value of others’
actions beyond signals by comparing the posterior RMSE of predicted probabilities relative
to the Bayesian benchmark under the signals and signals + actions specifications. Averaging
across rounds, incorporating others’ actions reduces RMSE by approximately 1 percentage
point. This reduction is driven by improved accuracy from round seven onward, where the
RMSE decreases by 1.5 percentage points.
Table K.3 reports the median RMSE estimates across scenarios. Overall, the largest
improvement in accuracy comes from incorporating signals, which reduces RMSE by approx-
imately 3 percentage points relative to the baseline scenario, with a particularly large effect
in later rounds (up to 6 percentage points). Beyond the information provided by signals,
incorporating the redundant information contained in others’ actions further improves par-
ticipants’ performance relative to the Bayesian benchmark, with an additional reduction in
RMSE of 1 percentage point, equivalent to one-third of the informational value of signals.

Heterogeneity in the Effect of Redundant Information
The main finding that participants perform better in the all treatment relative to the
signals treatment, as shown in Figure 1, reflects an average treatment effect that masks
heterogeneity across participants in their likelihood of making a correct bet. In this Appendix,
we show that the performance advantage of the all treatment over the signals treatment
is robust to conditioning on the distribution of prediction quality across participants.
For this purpose, we model the probability of making a correct bet at the individual
level using a flexible binary-response specification with individual-specific random effects.
For a given treatment (all or signals, the data generating process for the correct action
of participant i in round t of game g, vg

We leverage variation across rounds and games within participants to recover subject-
level response probabilities via Bayesian logistic regression. Using the posterior estimates
of individual probabilities, we replicate the analysis in Section 5.1, comparing how often
subjects correctly guess the state in each game round across treatments by quantiles of these
individual probabilities.
Figure L.1 summarizes these results. Consistent with the aggregate findings, subjects
across quantiles perform better in the all treatment relative to signals. Moreover, the
effect of redundant information is significantly larger for participants in the lower quantiles
of the distribution (i.e., the 5th, 10th, and 25th percentiles). Although the gap between
treatments is smaller at higher quantiles, it remains statistically significant and economically
meaningful (i.e., around 5 p.p.), particularly in earlier rounds.
Figure L.2 shows the full distribution of individual-level correct probabilities across
treatments and game rounds. Consistent with the aggregate findings, as the game progresses,
individuals in both signals and all treatments improve their performance. However, we
find substantial heterogeneity across participants, with individual probabilities ranging from
below 0.25 to above 0.95. Comparing treatments, we find that in later rounds (i.e., rounds
10, 15, and 20) a larger share of individuals performs better in the all treatment than in

Covariate Balance in Participant Characteristics
In Appendix F, we show that aggregate outcomes and individual-level behavior are very
similar and statistically indistinguishable across experimental sessions conducted in the
physical lab at UCSD and in the virtual lab at OSU. However, because half of the experimental
sessions in the all and signals treatments were conducted at different locations, with
distinct pools of college students (UCSD and OSU), we assess in this Appendix potential
imbalances in participants’ characteristics across treatments and their implications for
inference on individual behavior.
As a measure of covariate balance, Figure M.1 reports absolute standardized mean
differences between the all and signals treatments. We find almost no imbalance for the
constructed covariates overconfidence and risk (less than 0.1), moderate imbalance for
female and the constructed iq (less than 0.25), and substantial imbalance for STEM, with
31% of participants in the all treatment having a STEM major, compared to 21% in the
signals treatment.
We summarize the extent of imbalance across covariates by estimating the propensity
score, defined in our setting as
P [(]Ti = all | Xi),
74


## Page 75


where Xi is the vector of participant covariates (overconfidence, risk, female, iq, STEM).
We estimate the propensity score using a logistic regression of Ti on Xi.
Figure M.2 compares the distribution of the estimated propensity score between the
signals and all treatments by contrasting their quantiles across groups. The purple dots
lie consistently above the 45-degree line, indicating that participants in the all treatment
differ systematically from those in the signals treatment in their observable characteristics.
Based on the estimated propensity score, we implement one-to-one optimal matching.
Each of the 82 participants in the signals treatment is matched to one of the 152 participants
in the all treatment, yielding a total of 164 matched observations (82 matched pairs), with
70 unmatched participants in the all treatment.
The yellow triangles in Figure M.2, which lie close to the 45-degree line, indicate that
matching yields nearly identical propensity score distributions across the all and signals
treatments at most quantiles.

Random Actions in the Data
Our main analysis examines how individuals learn from others’ signals and actions, and
the extent to which their behavior deviates from the Bayesian optimum. In this Appendix,
we assess the extent to which such deviations are driven by participants who behave as if
random, ignoring available information. We focus on the none and signals treatments,
where relevant information is directly provided through observed signals.
To quantify random behavior, we estimate the effect of information Ii,t on individual
choices. We measure the information from signals with the posterior log-odds,
log-oddsit = log
 
Pr(ω = R | Ii,t)
Pr(ω = G | Ii,t)

which captures the relative evidence in favor of ω = R relative to ω = G.37 In particular,
under the none treatment, Ii,t = (si,τ)τ<t, whereas under the signals treatment, Ii,t =

The parameter of interest is βi, which captures participant i’s sensitivity to the posterior
log-odds. The term αi is a participant-specific random intercept, υg is a game-specific
random intercept, and λt is a round-specific random intercept. We assume

We estimate responsiveness to information using a Bayesian logistic regression. Within
this framework, we evaluate the posterior distribution of βi, focusing on whether it places
substantial mass near zero, consistent with random behavior or instead indicates learning,
i.e., βi > 0.
Figures N.4 and N.5 report the results of this estimation for the signals and none
treatments, respectively. Panel (a) in these figures reports the posterior change in the
probability of betting Red following a one-standard-deviation increase in the log-odds (in
favor of ω = R) across participants, corresponding to a homogeneous effect of information.
For both the signals and none treatments, we find a sizable effect of signals on behavior,
with an increase of approximately 19 percentage points in the probability of betting red.
However, this average effect masks substantial heterogeneity across participants. For more
than half of participants in both treatments, the effect of a one-standard-deviation increase
in log-odds favoring ω = R exceeds 25 percentage points.
On the other hand, around a quarter of participants in both treatments have posterior
95% credible intervals for βi that include zero, suggesting weak or no responsiveness to
information, consistent with random choices.
